GeoSWAC achieved substantially lower operational costs (up to 93.3% compared to the chiller- based system) and lower LCOC (up to 63.2% compared to the chiller-based system), driven by reduced electricity consumption and elimination of evaporative and blowdown water losses. Although GeoSWAC still requires electricity for pumping, its lower energy demand enhances system resilience, as the system can be sustained for longer periods with backup power sources, such as diesel generators or battery systems, offering continued cooling capacity during grid outages. The economic assessment of GeoSWAC systems relative to conventional chiller-based systems showed substantial reductions in both capital (10.6% to 13.6%) and operational costs (86.5% to 93.3%). These results indicate the economic potential of GeoSWAC technology based on initial assumptions and conceptual analysis, while acknowledging limitations such as operational and maintenance costs related to water chemistry effects, scaling, or corrosion and site-specific constraints, which should be addressed in future validation studies. The GeoSWAC concept benefits from two key assumptions: (1) access to an effectively infinite heat sink provided by deep seawater and (2) a favorable natural hydraulic gradient, which enables cold seawater to rise to sea level with minimal pumping. Pumping is only required from sea level to the building infrastructure, further reducing energy demand. Functionally similar to conventional SWAC, GeoSWAC reconfigures the system vertically (or with greater geometric freedom using directional drilling techniques) using inland wells instead of seabed pipelines. This design shifts constraints from ocean bathymetry to subsurface hydraulic connectivity offering potential advantages such as greater geographic flexibility and reduced sensitivity to weather during construction. 32 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. However, these benefits come with uncertainties, particularly related to subsurface conditions and potential flow rate limitations due to borehole diameter constraints. Overall, GeoSWAC represents a promising cooling solution for regions prone to power disruptions, where long-term resilience, water conservation, and reduced dependence on electricity are critical. Continued exploration of site feasibility, geologic suitability, and operational performance will be essential to unlocking its full potential. Future research could focus on validating key assumptions through site-specific performance modeling, deep geologic studies (e.g., exploratory drilling), and feasibility-level techno- economic analysis to quantify LCOC sensitivity to these variables.
